justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—are driven by the underlying trend in the variable I forecasted. At the 1-day horizon, the projection is heavily influenced by recent data and short-term dynamics, assuming minimal change from any major external factors in such a short timeframe. Consequently, the 1-day point estimate is very close to the most recent observed value. At the 1-week and 1-month horizons, the forecasts incorporate both the trend and momentum observed in recent data, as well as any seasonality or predictable patterns in the variable. The slight upward drift in the point estimates across the timeframes reflects either an expectation of steady growth or a reversion toward longer-term trends.

The widths of the confidence intervals (CIs) reflect growing uncertainty as time progresses. Over 1 day, the uncertainty is relatively small because abrupt changes are rare in that short window unless unusual events occur. As the forecast horizon shifts to 1 week and then to 1 month, uncertainty increases due to the compounding effects of small inaccuracies in the model, as well as the influence of more volatile or less predictable factors over time. This is why the 90% CI widens significantly from the 1-day to the 1-month forecast, capturing the greater range of plausible outcomes.

However, there are always risks or events that could push outcomes outside even the stated intervals. Unexpected shocks such as geopolitical events, large policy changes, extreme market disruptions, or unanticipated environmental factors could cause sudden departures from the predicted range. If these or other high-impact but low-probability events occur, they could invalidate the assumptions and dynamics underlying the forecast, introducing outcomes well outside even the 90% CI. Such risks are difficult to quantify precisely, but they are an inherent limitation of any forecasting model.
